quote: The correct view is that it does.
The human workers would be free to do other work, and, therefore, their capacities would not be weakened.
Machine-using does not weaken the capacity for thought; but it limits the need for it.
note: limits need for thought without weakening capacity

quote: The machine is thus a means of stimulating effort, and a means of saving it, but it does not diminish it.
note: use is optional; machine stimulates effort

quote: I think no one can doubt that it does so.
Neither is right, for machines do not create powers; they merely liberate them.
note: machines liberate unchanged powers into a new domain

quote: Just as the use of the bicycle or the motor-car has not lessened the vigor of the human body, so the use of machinery has not lessened the vigor of the human mind.
note: historical evidence: machine-age thinkers most original

quote: It is the tendency of the use of machines to weaken human capacities.
note: machines substitute less intelligent workers for more intelligent

quote: The latter view is, of course, the correct one.
Those who hold the latter view are right.
Thus the machines do not weaken the mind but increase its power and ability.
To rely upon machines is a weakness and a laziness.
The habit of using machines renders the human mind less capable of independent thought and action.
A machine is not an instrument of thought; it is an instrument of dependence; it is the substitute for thought.

Human capacities are not weakened by the use of machines, but are strengthened by the use of machines, because machines do not do the work by themselves, but are the means through which man’s intelligence and skill operate.
Therefore, the more we rely upon machines, the weaker do we become in the faculties of the soul.
The second statement is wrong, because it is only by relying on machines that man can have leisure to devote to the improvement of his capacities.
